title: One Awareness in Every Seat
hook: a packed bus home, and the same knowing in every seat
carry: one awareness, shiva, shines in every body
tomorrow: your mind wanders off mid-sit. where exactly did it go?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vijnana Bhairava caught a want at its first flicker and let it settle back where it came from. Today, the book looks up from the cushion, at everyone else.

The last bus home, packed to the doors. A nurse still in scrubs, asleep against the window. Two kids sharing one pair of earbuds. A man on the phone saying I know, I know, to someone who can't see him nod. Nobody looks at anybody. Each person is a whole world, sealed shut, riding the same bus. And a question floats up somewhere between stops: is the seeing behind each pair of eyes as private as it feels? The Vijnana Bhairava has a verse with an answer, and it's not the one the bus would suggest.
screen: `THE LAST BUS HOME.` → `EVERYONE SEALED IN.` → `HOW PRIVATE IS SEEING?`

segments.voice: Remember how this book began: the Goddess asked Bhairava what he really is, and instead of a description he gave her doors. Here's one, in plain words. The awareness of knower and known, someone seeing something, is common to everyone who has a body. What sets the practiced apart, Bhairava says, is attention to it. They notice the knowing itself; everyone else looks straight through it to the thing that's known. A neighboring verse goes further. A wanting, a knowing, the awareness of something as ordinary as a clay pot: these don't arise only in me, it says. They arise in others too. Hold that steadily, and a person becomes as wide as everything. Now the big teaching underneath, named plainly. In Kashmir Shaivism, the school that treasures this book, Shiva is consciousness itself: one awareness, shining in every being. It's a cousin of the Upanishads' old claim that the self in you, the atman, is not finally separate from Brahman, the one reality. So the nurse, the kids, the man on the phone aren't similar lamps in separate boxes. On this teaching, it's one light, in every seat. That's why many teachers read the everyday namaste, palms pressed together, as a bow to the divine in the other person. Notice the turn this run has taken. The breath, the fading sound, the first flicker of a want all happened inside one person. This door opens outward, to the stranger across the aisle who will never learn my name.
screen: `THE GODDESS ASKED; BHAIRAVA GAVE DOORS.` · `KNOWER AND KNOWN, IN EVERY BODY.` · `SHIVA IS CONSCIOUSNESS ITSELF.` · `NAMASTE: A BOW TO THE DIVINE IN YOU.` · then, large: `ONE AWARENESS IN EVERY SEAT.`

segments.voice: Listen for the farthest sound you can hear: traffic, a fan, a voice through a wall. Somewhere near that sound, someone else is hearing too. Rest in your own hearing, and let it sink in that the same plain knowing is lit in them right now.
The Vijnana Bhairava: a tantric book of doors. Today's door is the one awareness, Shiva himself in this school's teaching, lit in everyone who has a body.
For the road: one awareness, Shiva, shines in every body, even on the last bus home. Day sixteen twenty-five.
